analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to provide paid vacation earned at one hour per 25 hours worked.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, committee markup, or vote in the Senate and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require most employers to let workers earn paid vacation: one hour of paid leave for every 25 hours worked, up to 80 hours (10 days) in a 12-month period. Workers could use the leave for any reason, would be paid at their normal rate (tipped workers at least the full minimum wage), and would be paid out for unused leave if they leave the job. Employers could not fire or penalize someone for taking the leave, and the Labor Department and private lawsuits would enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of workers — especially low-wage and hourly workers in retail, food service, and hospitality — who currently get no paid vacation. The United States has no federal law guaranteeing any paid vacation, and lower-income workers are far less likely to have it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly and low-wage workers without paid vacation

how_it_helps.text: Employers must provide one hour of paid annual leave for every 25 hours worked, capped at 80 hours in a 12-month period, and workers begin earning it on day one.
Leave can be used for any reason starting 60 days after hire, and employers cannot require workers to say why they are taking it or to find their own shift coverage.
Leave is paid at the employee's normal rate; tipped employees must be paid at least the highest of federal, state, or local minimum wage while on leave.
Unused leave must be paid out at termination, and a worker rehired within 12 months gets previously earned leave reinstated.

It is unlawful to fire, discipline, or retaliate against a worker for using the leave, and workers can sue with attorney's fees covered, while the Labor Department gets FLSA-style investigative and subpoena authority.
The bill covers a broad range of employers under FLSA-style definitions, including public agencies, and guarantees existing union contracts or benefit plans that provide more leave are not cut back.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially those in retail, restaurants, hotels, and other sectors with many hourly workers, bear the cost of paid days off; some may raise prices, trim hours, or absorb the cost of covering absent workers.

drawbacks.text: The mandate costs employers money, and small or seasonal businesses could face real scheduling and cash-flow burdens; 10 days per year is a modest guarantee compared with mandates in other wealthy countries, but for a business with thin margins the cost is not trivial.
The cap of 80 hours a year means the benefit is small for part-time and low-hours workers — someone working 15 hours a week earns only about 31 hours of leave a year.

Employers can still impose limited, reasonable scheduling restrictions and reject requests for a bona fide business reason, so workers in tightly scheduled jobs may not be able to use the leave when they want.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: workers who currently get zero paid vacation gain guaranteed paid time off, with enforcement teeth. The costs fall on employers, who can manage with scheduling flexibility built into the bill, and the cap keeps the mandate modest. The main honest objection is the burden on small businesses and thin-margin employers, which the bill does not offset.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never held a hearing or voted on it, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sanders introduced the bill in the Senate on March 20, 2024, with Padilla joining as an original cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That was the bill's only action: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no action in the House before the Congress ended in January 2025.
Three cosponsors, all Democrats, signed on; no Republicans did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid for the leave, particularly hourly-service-sector businesses, are better off because the bill died; workers without paid vacation gained nothing. Sanders, who has championed this idea across multiple Congresses, keeps the issue alive for a future bill but this version left workers no better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have paid for the leave

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew only Democratic support — a Democratic-sponsored bill with three Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors — and it never advanced far enough for anyone to record a public vote against it.

industries.industry: Retail, restaurants, hotels, and other hourly service-sector employers
industries.note: These employers would bear the direct cost of guaranteed paid days off for workforces that often get no paid vacation today. Their interest in blocking the mandate runs directly against the workers the bill was written for.

Any employer meeting the FLSA-style coverage threshold (20 or more workweeks of employment) is covered, including small firms, and would face leave costs plus recordkeeping and notice requirements with no offsetting subsidy.

industries.industry: Employers with existing generous leave policies and unionized workplaces
industries.note: The bill forbids any cutback of contracts or benefit plans that already provide more leave, locking in better-than-mandate arrangements. These employers' interest runs alongside workers' here.
